claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by the absence of nanoscale precipitates or short-range chemical order.
The absence of dispersive or interfacial barriers permits less-constrained dislocation glide.
Less-constrained dislocation glide produces high ductility and machinability at the expense of yield strength and hardness.
The starting equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a single-phase solid solution with no significant nanoscale precipitates or ordering features.
Annealing followed by aging can induce nanoscale precipitates or enhanced short-range order in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi without changing its overall composition.
The induced precipitates or ordered domains act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The as-cast CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has low lattice distortion.
Dislocation motion in the as-cast alloy is relatively unimpeded because secondary phases are absent.
Heat-treatment-induced precipitates or ordering will force dislocations to interact with nanoscale obstacles.
Induced nanoscale precipitates or ordering will increase the yield strength and hardness relative to the starting alloy.
Induced nanoscale precipitates or ordering may reduce ductility relative to the starting alloy.
The mechanical properties can be tuned by controlling nanoscale obstacle density.
The hypothesis is restricted to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi, approximately 20 at.% of each element, tested near 25 °C under quasi-static tensile and compressive loading.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on precipitate or ordering-domain volume fraction, size, and distribution.
A lack of statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increases in the obstacle-containing condition would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The prediction and uncertainty fields say ductility only may decrease and that its response may vary, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to observe reduced ductility as falsifying the hypothesis.

The boundary limits tensile and compressive loading to yielding, but the hypothesis also proposes measuring and comparing ductility, which generally requires post-yield deformation and a defined terminal strain or fracture criterion.
